Another option would be that the record stating that he died two years earlier is unreliable. Is there any other option you could think of which we would have to consider.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that the information is unreliable, I can doubt the sources, the data sources that are being used. It is the BH army, the ministry of the BH army that is the data source here and there's no reason for me to doubt that, especially because in 1992 when the Prosecution expert used this, assessed it as a good data source. The possibility that something happened and that in that grave -- may I go on or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may go on although you are, rather, referring to the options I gave rather than to tell me whether there is any other option, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know I have to speculate whether there is something else or not. In the demographic office of the Prosecution, is there more documentation that I did not have an opportunity to see? I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you say that BiH Ministry of Defence information, that was considered to be reliable and therefore you have no reason to doubt that. Did I understand well that out of these 220 that some 80 were already corrected as being inaccurate? That's how I understand the evidence to be. Is that your understanding as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were corrected. But it's not the entire list as such that had been updated. That is to say that not everything had been corrected. Rather -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Some of them indeed remain still without answers or at least at the time. Now you earlier said that this was reliable, these were reliable lists, if for those where an answer has been received out of those 220, 80 have been corrected, whereas for quite a number of others, no additional information has yet been received. Would you still consider that reliable, that a rate of -- well, well over 30 per cent which where not all answers have been received, that 30 per cent was corrected and turned out have been unreliable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that the Prosecution expert considered that to be a highly reliable source when using it in 1992. This is a correction in relation to a particular figure, whereas this BH army lists contains, I cannot say anything now off the cuff, 20.000, 30.000, I don't know and 13.000 of which pertain to the region of Tuzla. So since the entire list was not reviewed, I cannot claim that it's 30 per cent of the total list of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you said more than that they presented it as reliable. Because what you said is the following: "In the BH army, the ministry of the BH army, that is the data source here, and there is no reason for me to doubt that, especially ..." So apart from it being presented as reliable information, pointing at well over 30 per cent having been corrected, although not all answers had yet been received, you consider that it's still -- there's no reason to -- well, at least have some concerns about the reliability or have some doubts about the reliability if that number of cases have been corrected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This number of corrections pertains to the 220 that we're looking at here, not the total list of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that Dr. Tabeau in 1992 assessed as good and reliable. Not me. I have no reason to doubt that assessment of hers, so it is not 30 per cent of corrections in the total list. It 30 per cent of corrections in this list that was presented. Namely that these persons are also on the Prosecution list and the BH claims it was earlier on, that they had lost their lives earlier on, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now again, not wanting to look at names but if we look at the fourth entry from the top of the page, and the ICMP protocol number is 1602/03, we see for that individual under the date of death, military, the notation 1001994. Now, in commenting about this type of notation, of which there are several on this page, Dr. Tabeau says as follows on transcript page 19439, lines 19 through 24 on a question posed by Judge Moloto -- I should read the question too. That's at line 16. "JUDGE MOLOTO: That is true, but when one looks at the list, there are those with a double zero and there are those with a single zero. "THE WITNESS: I would interpret this as a 101 being an incomplete code 1/00/1, and I would interpret this dating exact day way, meaning that the date is incomplete. Day and month are unavailable and the only part available is the year 1994. It is a typo that you often see in these kind of situations. Somebody who was typing in the 101994 just skipped one zero simply." Do you agree with Dr. Tabeau interpretation that for these entries 1001994 or 101994 we only know the date of -- pardon me, the year of death, 1994. Is that how you would read this data.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean 101946? Is that what you mean? The fourth case from the top?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The very next column that says 1001994.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is interpretation. These -- this is the way data are registered. It means that it pertains to the 10th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, do you have any explanation as to why so many people apparently then died on the 10th of January, 1994? What would have happened that all those mismatches that they all had died on the 10th of January, 1994? I see them by the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know whether there was some fighting then or something. I really cannot say. I presume that it's the army that knows what that was all about. Whether on those dates there were some particular battles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You do not know, but has it raised any concern that suddenly many, many persons which were reported to have found in mass graves in Srebrenica massively died on the 10th of January, 1994? Did it raise any concern on your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see it being en masse here as compared to the rest. It did not raise any concerns in my mind because it is an official state document. That was my starting point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought they made sure it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say you don't see it as being en masse. How many are there on the list which appears on your screen that died on the 10th of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not count them but these are the examples of those I found back then. There must have been more than 220. I didn't count them, but I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You already formed an opinion that it was not en masse whereas we see many, many of them already on this first page and you said you didn't count them but you commented it was en masse. I'll count them and then we'll know approximately what percentage it is -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to make sure we understand each other. It may be a lot as -- as compared to 220 but I don't know whether it is a mass occurrence compared to 13 or 15.000 it is well likely that it is significant occurrence compared to the initial figure. I didn't or wasn't able to examine everything in details. These are just examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that parties agree that many many persons apparently reported as having died on the 10 -- the 1001994.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 10 if you count the ones that are with the corrected date of death. Ten or 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I said if you take the corrected date of death, Your Honour. It's 11; trust me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... by Judge Orie in relation to the many people died on that day ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... according to the ABiH lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the date has been corrected they did not die on that day they died on a different day. Isn't that correct as well, Your Honour. The question that has been asked by Judge Orie, the answer is 10 or 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The concern was about the initially reported date of death and some have been clarified. Others have not been clarified. But initially apparently it was reported for many many of them that they would have died on that day. Which the witness says is the 10th of January. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We don't need this document on the screen anymore unless Your Honours have something further with it. I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We don't need anything at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to now move to some items that you were asked about in court. If we could first have P7520 in e-court. You were asked about this today. This is from the public security station in Prijedor from the MUP, the Ministry of Interior. First of all, Professor, in relation to a properly conducted census in your experience, is the Ministry of Interior the organ that undertakes to collect data for a census.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it has never been the case. It is well known who is supposed to correct data for a census and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I'd like to go to a different topic and for that, I'd like to have P1900, page 85 in the ... one moment. It should be, I think, page 85 in the Serbian -- in the English and page 90 in the Serbian. Yes, that's the page. Now, while this page was shown to you yesterday in court, you were asked a question and you were not -- you were in the middle of answering when your answer was cut off. I'm going to read the question and the answer that we have thus far and then I'll give you an opportunity to complete your answer. And this starts at transcript page 38363, line 5: "Q. I'll ask another question. You are aware that once these 1.15 million individuals had their records matched, they would be excluded from the next round of matching; correct? "A. Well, if he got all the matchings, it's logical he let them out. He would say, I got 55 per cent of exact matches. I'm leaving out the rest but I have to --" And then you were interrupted and then you continued: "... make a little introduction. The Prosecutor is asking me bit by bit not the whole. The reference here is to the comparison of census and voters' registers. These two lists do not contain the same data but they would have one thing in common: The MB number. The voters' register does not have the name of father and the ethnicity. It does contain name and surname, date of birth and the MB number where it exists. The census contains the MB number if it's good, the date of birth, ethnicity, name, surname, and father's name ..." And then you were interrupted. And then you continued: "... if you go about matching -- I have to explain this because this is a special system of matching ..." And then you were interrupted. And then you continued: "Judge, Your Honour, if they don't contain the same data, there could be two stages of matching for the same matching. I took the MB number from the voters' register. I have to explain this because we have a misunderstanding here. The Prosecutor doesn't understand me. If you take the MB number from the voters' register, and by that number you find Svetlana Radovanovic ..." And then you were interrupted and we don't have the rest of your explanation. Could you please try to complete your explanation.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although the OTP experts do not explain it directly, they only say when comparing the voters' register and the census as specified in the methodology applied to the Slobodan Milosevic case report, they engage in several steps. The several steps do not necessarily refer to the key used for the matching but to the difference between the characteristics of the census, on the one hand, and the voters' register on the other. The voters' register does not contain the name of father and ethnicity. It does contain first name, last name and an MB number. The census contains the first name, father's name, last name, and ethnicity, and there may or may not be an MB number. If they match according to the correct MB without saying there are 60 per cent of correct MBs in the census and in the register, then if they only rely on the MB, that is to say, exclusively on numbers amounting to the best way of matching under the condition, then the MB numbers are correct, then they come up with real persons such as Svetlana Radovanovic. If her number on the voters' register is correct, it will match the same MB number, if correct, in the census. And then they have this Svetlana Radovanovic whose father's name is Dragan born on this and that date and her ethnicity is as follows. If the MB is incorrect, they can look for Svetlana Radovanovic according to her year or date of birth. They may find her or not and then they can shorten and say let's just take the year not the whole date. Then they can get certain overlaps or matches which are not direct because they will have a number of names, different people who shared the name of Svetlana, last name Radovanovic and who were perhaps born in the same year. Then out of the several people, they need to choose the Svetlana that they need. Once all that is done, they can say, This part that we think is a match will no longer be matched because according to these elements we cannot find them all. So that's the statistics I referred to. They could have said, according to the first criterion, we matched 20 per cent, then we matched 10 per cent and then the 30 per cent were done according to the first criterion and after the several steps we have undertaken, we will no longer be using them in the further matching process. The matching process as specified according to Dr. Tabeau in terms of the steps they took, i.e., according to the rules provided by Dr. Brunborg with Dr. Tabeau being the co-author, well, I have to make a correction now because I'm not certain about this as it is not explained anywhere. When it says five it doesn't mean it refers to the fifth rule alone but it may well be a combination. It may refer only to the IQ value number 5. Now when taking into account all those rules 1 through 5 because Dr. Brunborg obviously says that values 5 and 3 are considered good matches, then by using those, they matched some 1.5 million voters against the census. But let me remind you that there are 2.7 million voters as Dr. Brunborg specified in the report. And yesterday the Prosecutor showed me the precise figures for the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina which are 2.65 or so million. If you accept these criteria and match them to come up with the figure of 1.5, it is no longer, 70 -- 79.5 per cent compared to the overall voters' register. It is only 50-plus per cent. So from the assertion that the percentage is 79, we go down to the lower figure but they give a certain probability greater than 2, for example, leaving out again the statistics of comparison. Why? Because it displays the level of -- or -- or amount of combinations they have relied upon. That is what I tried to explain yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can move to another part, at transcript page 38353, you had started answering the following question which I will read, starting at line 6: "So my question to you is: It is not unique or rare for statisticians to encounter an error rate in the underlying raw data that is well in excess of 5 per cent; correct?" Your expert, Dr. Tabeau, also explains that in the methodology provided for the report in the Mladic case, and she says hardly any country, if any, she doesn't say which one does it, rarely carries out matching at individual levels as far as population censuses are concerned. Please, of course, I'm paraphrasing. I cannot say exactly but I can bring it in later because data protection is very important there. So it's done according to..." And then you were not allowed to finish. So could you please explain for us the entirety of your answer so that we have the benefit of the same in the record.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is done at certain levels. For example, an aggregate whole need not cover an entire country but maybe a part of it. It is practice in all developed countries as well as some others for the simple reason that individual data must never be published. Nothing is done at an individual level because it amounts to official secret. Such data is secret. When something like that is done in the US and the most developed countries, it is precisely regulated. Dr. Tabeau says plainly in the rest of the paragraph that they opted for the individual level.

That is not my job here. I'm trying to explain that the methodology that was applied exists only in the demographic unit of the The Hague Tribunal and no where else in the professional and scientific world.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The JMBG is short for unique identification citizen number. All citizens of the former Yugoslavia under the 1982 or 1983 law were assigned a JMBG. Even if there are people with same first and last name and date of birth their MB is not the same. It is differentiated according to the other characteristics. Since 1982, every person born had to be assigned an MB and only then was the person recorded in the register of births.

utterances.text: We would inform the command of the Ilidza Brigade, that is to say, the army. We did not have the possibility to fire at the other side. So the army was notified, and also these observers of the UN peace mission, through our liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did the members of the Army of Republika Srpska neutralise those firing points?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably as one does in war, by weaponry and --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's another leading question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you refrain from leading, Mr. Lukic. And perhaps rephrase that question, although partly answered already.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the position of Ilidza at that time? From how many sides was it surrounded by members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, another one, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, another one. We're not here on a course, Mr. Lukic. We are here in the examination-in-chief of a witness. Would you please not forget about what was in the course, but, rather, practice it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Ilidza Brigade, which units was it facing at the front line?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the other side, there were units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was the 1st Sarajevo Corps on one side and on the other side there was, I think, the 3rd Corps that covered the Doboj region. That is to say, there were BH army members on two sides, and on the third side members of the HVO. These are the lines towards Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said what the situation was like at Ilidza. What about the other municipalities, the Sarajevo municipalities that were under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two parts of Serb territory. Part of Serb territory is Hadzici, Ilidza, Rajlovac, Vogosca, Ilijas and they were on the western side of the Sarajevo field and then this other territory, under VRS control or Serb authority's control and that is Novo Sarajevo, part of municipality of Novi Grad and also part of the municipality of Ilidza. That was in that area that Hrasnica, Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija cut through it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dobrinje, Mojmilo. So divided into two parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are invited to slow down. Otherwise part of your words might be lost. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there are two parts of the territory of the city of Sarajevo. As I already mentioned, five municipalities were at the lower part and then there were these three other municipalities in the upper part. So it was divided into two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who had under their control the part of Sarajevo that was called Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of Grbavica was under the control of the VRS or, rather, the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which part of Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I had a map here, I could show you that from one street to the other. And it is -- I mean, if we look down the Miljacka river, it's on the left-hand side, underneath Vrbanja Bridge, all the way up to the Bridge of Brotherhood and Unity.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see now video 1D06006C.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we stop here, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We saw the beginning of this video-clip. Can you tell us which part of town this is.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Grbavica, because I was in Grbavica very often during the war and otherwise I do know the entire area of Sarajevo. I worked as a policeman in Sarajevo before the war during the war, after the war, so I see clearly that this is the neighbourhood of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we continue, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are we supposed to ignore the sound or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, of course, not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I mean, the spoken words, not perhaps the sounds which doesn't need translation, but the comment spoken by the broadcast system. Should we pay attention to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, that's -- that irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's irrelevant, so we don't need any translation of comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just the sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just the sound. Not words spoken by the broadcast station. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the sound doesn't matter for what we saw just now, I would like to ask you also to disregard what you heard when this video-clip was played. You told us that you meant that you recognised this as Grbavica, part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Out of these buildings that were shown in the video just now, how far away is the front line?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 200 to 300 metres, maximum. Somewhere it's perhaps even less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Lukic, there is a bit of a problem. I mean, the comment you say is irrelevant. At the same time but perhaps I should be clear to that, the witness listens to it and could be guided by it, be influenced by it, and if you later say you should ignore it, that is not the proper way. Of course, what you should have done is to switch off the sound entirely but then, of course, we would have lost also the running of the children, et cetera. So, one way or another, this is not a very satisfactory situation you have created, but for the time being, since Ms. Edgerton was not on her feet, let's move on for the time being. And if you are talking about buildings, how far they are, that, of course, would then cover all the buildings and I have seen at least six or seven already. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll try to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the street that was filmed with this camera, how far away is the front line?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, 200 to 300 metres. You see, you can disregard anything that was heard in these videos because I saw a lot of this during the course of my work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, there's no need to tell us what we could disregard. Mr. Lukic, I'm also looking at the clock. I see that the clip is almost at its end. Unless you could promise us that in one or two minutes we'll be fished. Otherwise, we would wait until Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll wait until Monday. No problem. It is better to be realistic than to ... Mr. Tusevljak, and I must perhaps -- well, perhaps not correct myself, but be more precise, when I said good afternoon, Mr. Tusevljak, I should have made clear that it's Mr. Simo Tusevljak who is known as (redacted) in this case, and not any other Mr. Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there is no translation in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, I'll say again what I just -- it's there? I should have been more precise when I said good afternoon, Mr. Tusevljak. I should have made it clear that I said good afternoon to Mr. Simo Tusevljak, who is known as (redacted) in this case and not any other Mr. Tusevljak. Having put this on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday you had indicated we should not use GRM numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. At least not the old ones. I stand corrected for that, and I'm asking for a redaction as far as the number is concerned. We adjourn for the day, and we'll not resume until Monday. Mr. Tusevljak, therefore, we'd like to see back on Monday, the 31st of August, 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, I. You are invited to follow the usher, but not until after I have instructed you that should not speak or communicate in whatever way, as you have not done in the past few months, not to communicate or speak with anyone about your testimony, whether it is given today or earlier in July or still to be given next week. If that is clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we resume Monday, the 31st of August, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
